title: Between the lines
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A HINT IS A DESCRIPTION THAT STOPS. The ordinary Korean way to ask for what you are not entitled to ask for is to name the situation and say nothing else. bang-i jom chumneyo is close the window.
JOM IS NOT A LITTLE HERE. L2-M1's jom is the marker that turns a description into a request. Take it out and the same sentence is a complaint about the room.
-NEYO FRAMES IT AS JUST NOTICED. L5-M3's ending is the whole difference between a hint and a grievance: you have observed the cold, not held anybody responsible for it.

V-(EU)LKKAYO OFFERS INSTEAD OF ASKING. Shall I? is a question about yourself, and so the least intrusive request the language has. L2-M6's -(eu)llaeyo invites the other person; this one volunteers you.
AN ENGLISH SPEAKER HINTS BY CHOICE, A KOREAN SPEAKER BY DEFAULT. Anything directed upward is hinted, so saving hints for delicate moments leaves you blunt for the rest of the day.

KOREAN SARCASM IS A FLAT POSITIVE SENTENCE. Learn to hear it and never attempt it: English-shaped sarcasm in Korean is heard as sincere or as rude, never as funny. This course teaches its reception only.
NUNCHI IS THE SKILL ITSELF, and Korean has a name for it. nunchi-ga isseoyo is reads the room; nunchi-ga eopseoyo is the standard thing said about somebody who does not.
JOM GEURAEYO IS A NO. Two words that mean nothing apart — a bit, it is that way — and together decline. L4-M5's jom eoryeoul geot gatayo is the fuller version and stays L4-M5's.

sentences.cue: It is a bit cold in here.

words.note: The room you are both standing in — which is why it can carry a request without one being made.

sentences.trap: English hears this as small talk about the weather indoors. In Korean it is the request, delivered whole, and an answer of yes, it is is a refusal.

variations.changed: jom dropped: an observation, and no longer a request

variations.cue: The room, at least, is a bit cold.
variations.changed: -eun for -i: the room set against something else

mistake.why: Without -neyo the sentence states a fact you already knew, which reads as a complaint. -neyo says you have only just noticed, and that is what keeps the request light.

sentences.usage: Asking somebody senior to close a window without asking.
sentences.mnemonic: Say the room, not the favour.

words.note: A question you ask about yourself, so nothing is asked of anybody else. Attach -lkkayo to the same stem that takes L2-M1's su.

sentences.trap: English shall I? is stiff and old-fashioned; Korean -(eu)lkkayo is the everyday way to volunteer, and reaching instead for a plain I will do it takes the choice away from the person you are offering to.

variations.changed: galkkayo for halkkayo: the same offer on a motion verb
a consonant stem, so -eulkkayo takes the linking vowel

mistake.why: L2-M6's -(eu)llaeyo asks what somebody else wants, so turning it on yourself asks your own preference out loud. The offer needs -(eu)lkkayo.

sentences.usage: Volunteering for a job nobody has assigned.

sentences.cue: Do you happen to have a moment?

words.note: L1-M3's isseoyo carrying L3-M8's -si- for the person you are asking. The honorific is on them, never on your own time.

sentences.trap: English do you have a minute is already the whole request. So is this one — but hoksi is what makes it escapable, and dropping it turns a soft opening into a summons.

variations.changed: hoksi dropped: still polite, but no longer escapable

variations.cue: Do you happen to have a moment?
variations.changed: the honorific removed: for somebody your own age

mistake.why: The honorific raises whoever the sentence is about, and here that has to be the listener. Putting yourself in the subject slot raises you instead.

sentences.usage: Opening a request you are prepared to have refused.
sentences.mnemonic: hoksi leaves the door open; -seyo bows on the way in.

sentences.cue: My friend reads a room well.

words.note: Korean's own name for the skill this module teaches: seeing what has not been said. It is had or not had, never done.

sentences.trap: English tact is about what you choose to say. nunchi is about what you manage to hear, so it is praised in a listener, not in a speaker.

variations.cue: My friend cannot read a room.
variations.changed: eopseoyo for isseoyo: the standard complaint
-reul with L2-M6's bwayo: watching for the unsaid

mistake.why: nunchi is not something you do. Korean has it or lacks it — nunchi-ga isseoyo, nunchi-ga eopseoyo — and only nunchi-reul bwayo puts it in motion.

sentences.usage: Saying why somebody is easy or hard to be around.
sentences.mnemonic: nun is the eye; nunchi is what the eye picks up.

sentences.cue: The window is open. It is a bit cold in here.

words.note: The thing the hint is really about. Naming it and then naming the cold is the whole request, in two sentences and no verbs of asking.

sentences.trap: English would join these with so — the window is open, so it is cold. Korean leaves the join out on purpose: the gap between the two sentences is where the request sits.

variations.changed: -eul for -i: somebody did it, rather than it being so
the second half withheld: a fact, and no request

mistake.why: Finishing the thought destroys it. Once the instruction is spoken the hint has become an order, and a polite ending does not undo that.

sentences.usage: Two flat observations, laid side by side for somebody to act on.
sentences.mnemonic: State the window, state the cold, stop talking.

sentences.cue: I was just asking. It is fine.

words.note: It removes the motive from what you just said, which is how a hint is taken back when it has landed too hard.

sentences.trap: English just minimises the thing itself — it is just a question. geunyang says the question had no purpose behind it, which is the part that lets everybody off.

variations.changed: the asking dropped: a refusal of the offer
geunyang gone, and with it the way out

mistake.why: dwaesseoyo is curt where this sentence is trying to be kind, and L4-M2 already spent it on -ge dwaesseoyo, it came about. The polite decline is L2-M1's gwaenchanayo.

sentences.usage: Withdrawing a hint the moment it makes somebody uncomfortable.
sentences.mnemonic: geunyang empties the sentence of its reason.

sentences.cue: How on earth did you do it so well?

words.note: Marks the sentence as an exclamation rather than a question. Said warmly it is real praise; said flat over a mistake it is the sarcasm to recognise and not to copy.

sentences.trap: The words are positive either way, and a course with no sound cannot show you the flat delivery that flips them. Hear this one; produce only the warm reading.

variations.cue: How on earth do you do it so well?
variations.changed: the honorific present: praise to somebody senior

variations.cue: Did you do it that well?
variations.changed: eojjeom dropped: a plain question, and no exclamation at all

mistake.why: Spelling the criticism out is not sarcasm in Korean, it is an insult. The flat delivery of the positive sentence is the whole device, and this is why a learner should only ever receive it.

sentences.usage: Reading a compliment that may not be one.
sentences.mnemonic: eojjeom throws its hands up — in delight, or not.

words.note: Layered on top of L3-M3's geot gatayo, it puts one more step between you and the thing you are about to decline.

sentences.trap: English probably reports a likelihood. Here it reports nothing about the world at all — it is distance, and the sentence it is attached to is a no.

variations.cue: It seems it would be difficult.
variations.changed: ama dropped: L4-M5's refusal at its own strength
the same hedge over an acceptance

mistake.why: The hedge and the flat no cancel each other. If the answer is going to be refused outright, ama only makes it sound evasive; keep the hedge for the sentence that never says no.

sentences.usage: Declining something you have not been formally asked for.
sentences.mnemonic: ama steps back one pace before the sentence even starts.

sentences.cue: That one is... a bit, you know.

words.note: Learn it whole. Neither word says no — a bit, it is like that — and together they are the everyday decline for an idea you will not name a fault in.

sentences.trap: English needs the adjective — it is a bit much, a bit expensive. Korean deliberately never supplies it, and supplying one turns a decline into a criticism.

variations.cue: This one is a bit, you know.
variations.changed: the near demonstrative: the thing in your hand

variations.cue: It is a bit, you know.
variations.changed: the subject dropped, as it usually is

mistake.why: This is a perfectly good sentence and a different act: it names the problem. jom geuraeyo refuses without naming one, which is what leaves the other person's idea intact.

sentences.usage: Turning down a suggestion in front of the person who made it.
sentences.mnemonic: A bit... that way. Nobody has to finish it.

sentences.cue: The mood in here is not good. Let us just go.

words.note: The thing nunchi reads. Naming it is how two people agree about a room without either of them saying what happened in it.

sentences.trap: English says the mood is off and then explains. Korean names the mood and moves, and the explanation would be the rude part.

variations.cue: The mood in here is good.
variations.changed: the positive: the same reading, reported warmly
-reul with bwayo: the mood as something to watch

mistake.display: Bunwigi-ga an joayo. Waenyahamyeon sajangnim-i hwa-ga nasseoyo.
mistake.script: 분위기가 안 좋아요. 왜냐하면 사장님이 화가 났어요.
mistake.why: L5-M6's bracket is exactly wrong here. A hint that supplies its own reason has stopped being a hint, and naming the person is what makes it repeatable against you.

sentences.usage: Getting a friend out of a room without saying why.
sentences.mnemonic: bunwigi is the weather in the room.

comprehensionPool.cue: It is a bit cold in here.
Do you happen to have a moment?
How on earth did you do it so well?
That one is a bit, you know.
The mood in here is not good.
My friend reads a room well.
